claim: The equid family has provided textbook examples of macroevolutionary changes due to its exceptionally rich fossil record.
source: The exceptionally rich fossil record available for the equid family has provided textbook examples of macroevolutionary changes.
evidence: This is a general statement about the equid fossil record that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Horses, asses, and zebras represent three extant subgenera of the Equus lineage.
source: Horses, asses, and zebras represent three extant subgenera of Equus lineage, while the Sussemionus subgenus is another remarkable Equus lineage ranging from North America to Ethiopia in the Pleistocene.
evidence: This is a statement of established taxonomic classification.

claim: The Sussemionus subgenus ranged from North America to Ethiopia in the Pleistocene.
source: Horses, asses, and zebras represent three extant subgenera of Equus lineage, while the Sussemionus subgenus is another remarkable Equus lineage ranging from North America to Ethiopia in the Pleistocene.
evidence: This is supported by the fossil record and previous research.

claim: 26 archaeological specimens from Northern China in the Holocene were sequenced and assigned morphologically and genetically to Equus ovodovi.
source: We sequenced 26 archaeological specimens from Northern China in the Holocene that could be assigned morphologically and genetically to Equus ovodovi, a species representative of Sussemionus.
evidence: This is directly supported by the sequencing data and morphological analysis presented in the study.

claim: The first high-quality complete genome of the Sussemionus lineage was sequenced to 13.4× depth of coverage.
source: We present the first high-quality complete genome of the Sussemionus lineage, which was sequenced to 13.4× depth of coverage.
evidence: This is directly supported by the genomic sequencing data presented in the study.

claim: Radiocarbon dating demonstrates that the Sussemionus lineage survived until ~3500 years ago.
source: Radiocarbon dating demonstrates that this lineage survived until ~3500 years ago, despite continued demographic collapse during the Last Glacial Maximum and the great human expansion in East Asia.
evidence: This is supported by radiocarbon dating results presented in the study.

claim: The Sussemionus lineage experienced continued demographic collapse during the Last Glacial Maximum.
source: Radiocarbon dating demonstrates that this lineage survived until ~3500 years ago, despite continued demographic collapse during the Last Glacial Maximum and the great human expansion in East Asia.
evidence: This is supported by demographic modeling (PSMC) presented in the study.

claim: Sussemionus diverged from the ancestor of non-caballine equids ~2.3–2.7 million years ago.
source: We also confirmed the Equus phylogenetic tree and found that Sussemionus diverged from the ancestor of non-caballine equids ~2.3–2.7 million years ago and possibly remained affected by secondary gene flow post-divergence.
evidence: This is supported by G-PhoCS demographic modeling presented in the study.

claim: Sussemionus possibly remained affected by secondary gene flow post-divergence.
source: We also confirmed the Equus phylogenetic tree and found that Sussemionus diverged from the ancestor of non-caballine equids ~2.3–2.7 million years ago and possibly remained affected by secondary gene flow post-divergence.
evidence: This is supported by D-statistics and G-PhoCS analyses showing evidence of admixture.

claim: Small genetic diversity, rather than enhanced inbreeding, limited the species' chances of survival.
source: We found that the small genetic diversity, rather than enhanced inbreeding, limited the species' chances of survival.
evidence: This is supported by heterozygosity and ROH analyses presented in the study.

claim: The genus Equus emerged in North America some 4.0–4.5 million years ago.
source: It emerged in North America some 4.0–4.5 million years ago (Orlando et al., 2013), and first spread into Eurasia ~2.6 million years ago (Mya), via the Beringia land bridge (Lindsay et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Orlando et al., 2013.

claim: Equus first spread into Eurasia ~2.6 million years ago via the Beringia land bridge.
source: It emerged in North America some 4.0–4.5 million years ago (Orlando et al., 2013), and first spread into Eurasia ~2.6 million years ago (Mya), via the Beringia land bridge (Lindsay et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lindsay et al., 1980.

claim: The first vicariance and expansion out of America led to the emergence of the ancestors of zebras, hemiones, and donkeys.
source: This first vicariance and expansion out of America led to the emergence of the ancestors of zebras, hemiones, and donkeys, a group collectively known as non-caballine (or stenonine) equids.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic understanding and fossil evidence.

claim: Another expansion through Beringia occurred ~0.8–1.0 Mya allowing caballine equids to enter into the Old World.
source: Another expansion through Beringia occurred ~0.8–1.0 Mya (Vershinina et al., 2021), which allowed caballine equids (i.e., those most closely related to the horse) to enter into the Old World, where they persisted until the modern era and were domesticated ~5500–4200 years ago (Gaunitz et al., 2018; Librado et al., 2021; Outram et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vershinina et al., 2021.

claim: Caballine equids were domesticated ~5500–4200 years ago.
source: Another expansion through Beringia occurred ~0.8–1.0 Mya (Vershinina et al., 2021), which allowed caballine equids (i.e., those most closely related to the horse) to enter into the Old World, where they persisted until the modern era and were domesticated ~5500–4200 years ago (Gaunitz et al., 2018; Librado et al., 2021; Outram et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gaunitz et al., 2018; Librado et al., 2021; Outram et al., 2009.

claim: Ancient DNA data have revealed that the genetic diversity of non-caballine Equus was considerably larger in the past than it is today.
source: In the recent years, ancient DNA (aDNA) data have revealed that the genetic diversity of non-caballine Equus was considerably larger in the past than it is today (Librado and Orlando, 2021; Orlando, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Librado and Orlando, 2021; Orlando, 2020.

claim: The Sussemiones lineage radiated across North America, Africa, and Siberia.
source: This lineage radiated across North America, Africa, and Siberia, and developed multiple adaptations to a whole range of arid and humid environments (Eisenmann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eisenmann, 2010.

claim: Sussemiones developed multiple adaptations to a whole range of arid and humid environments.
source: This lineage radiated across North America, Africa, and Siberia, and developed multiple adaptations to a whole range of arid and humid environments (Eisenmann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eisenmann, 2010.

claim: Sussemiones were first believed to have become extinct during the Middle Pleistocene as the last known specimen dated back to ~500 kya in southeastern Siberia, Russia.
source: Sussemiones were first believed to have become extinct during the Middle Pleistocene as the last known specimen showing typical morpho-anatomical characters dated back to ~500 kya (thousand years ago) in southeastern Siberia, Russia (Vasiliev, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vasiliev, 2013.

claim: DNA results indicated that the Sussemiones lineage survived until the Late Pleistocene.
source: However, DNA results obtained on multiple osseous remains within the radiocarbon range and showing morphological traits reminiscent of the Eurasian Sussemiones species indicated that the lineage in fact survived until the Late Pleistocene (Druzhkova et al., 2017; Orlando et al., 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Druzhkova et al., 2017; Orlando et al., 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2019.

claim: Early publications indicated Sussemiones survival dates of 40–50 kya in southeastern Siberia, Russia (Proskuryakova cave).
source: Early publications indicated survival dates 40–50 kya in southeastern Siberia, Russia (Proskuryakova cave) (Orlando et al., 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013), ~32 kya at the Denisova cave (Druzhkova et al., 2017), and ~12.6 kya at northeastern China (Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Orlando et al., 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013.

claim: Sussemiones survived until ~32 kya at the Denisova cave.
source: Early publications indicated survival dates 40–50 kya in southeastern Siberia, Russia (Proskuryakova cave) (Orlando et al., 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013), ~32 kya at the Denisova cave (Druzhkova et al., 2017), and ~12.6 kya at northeastern China (Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Druzhkova et al., 2017.

claim: Sussemiones survived until ~12.6 kya at northeastern China.
source: Early publications indicated survival dates 40–50 kya in southeastern Siberia, Russia (Proskuryakova cave) (Orlando et al., 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013), ~32 kya at the Denisova cave (Druzhkova et al., 2017), and ~12.6 kya at northeastern China (Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2019.

claim: Previous studies showed that Sussemiones formed a non-caballine lineage that may have diverged first from the lineage ancestral to zebras, hemiones, and donkeys.
source: These studies showed that Sussemiones formed a non-caballine lineage that may have diverged first from the lineage ancestral to zebras, hemiones, and donkeys.
evidence: This is based on previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: The exact placement of Sussemiones could not be fully resolved and has remained contentious.
source: However, the exact placement of Sussemiones could not be fully resolved and has remained contentious (Heintzman et al., 2017; Orlando et al., 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Heintzman et al., 2017; Orlando et al., 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013.

claim: Archaeological excavations were carried out in three Holocene sites in China: Honghe, Muzhuzhuliang, and Shatangbeiyuan.
source: In this study, we have carried out archaeological excavations in three Holocene sites in China (Honghe, Heilongjiang Province; Muzhuzhuliang, Shaanxi Province; Shatangbeiyuan, Ningxia Province) (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1a) and uncovered equine samples showing morphological features that may be characteristic of Sussemiones.
evidence: This is directly supported by the archaeological work described in the study and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Honghe site was dated to ~3400–4400 years ago and belonged to a unique, rich fishing and hunting culture characteristic of northeastern China.
source: At the Honghe site (47.20°N, 123.62°E), excavation fieldwork of nearly 20,000 m2 has uncovered a late Neolithic settlement site dated to ~3400–4400 years ago, which belonged to a unique, rich fishing and hunting culture characteristic of northeastern China (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by archaeological dating and cultural analysis.

claim: The Muzhuzhuliang site belonged to the 'Longshan culture' and was dated to ~3800–4300 years ago.
source: The Muzhuzhuliang site (38.83°N, 110.50°E) belonged to the 'Longshan culture.' It was dated to ~3800–4300 years ago and represents the most complete moated settlement hitherto excavated in the late Neolithic age of Northern China, showing a mixed subsistence economy involving agriculture, animal husbandry, and hunting (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by archaeological dating and cultural analysis, with a citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: The Shatangbeiyuan site belonged to the early cultural relics of Neolithic 'Qijia culture' and was dated to ~3900–4200 years ago.
source: Finally, the Shatangbeiyuan site (35.63°N, 105.11°E) belonged to the early cultural relics of Neolithic 'Qijia culture,' which was dated to ~3900–4200 years ago.
evidence: This is supported by archaeological dating and cultural analysis.

claim: No obvious signs of domestication were found amongst the equine specimens investigated at the three sites.
source: No obvious signs of domestication, including paleopathologies related to horseback riding, bridling, or chariotry (Bendrey, 2007; Taylor and Tuvshinjargal, 2018), were found amongst the equine specimens investigated at the three sites.
evidence: This is based on morphological examination of the specimens.

claim: Slash marks and indications of bone marrow extraction were found on some of the bones, suggesting that these specimens were hunted.
source: In contrast, slash marks could be identified on some of the bones (HH13H, HH26H, and MZ104H), together with indications of bone marrow extraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). These findings suggest that these specimens were hunted.
evidence: This is based on morphological examination of the specimens shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All the equine specimens investigated showed morphological and genetic signatures distinct from those of extant horses and donkeys.
source: All the equine specimens investigated in this study showed morphological and genetic signatures (short fragments of the mitochondrial hypervariable region) distinct from those of extant horses and donkeys (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by morphological and genetic analysis.

claim: The morphological differences were especially marked in the second and third molars, which appeared to be smaller than in modern horses.
source: The morphological differences were especially marked in the second and third molars, which appeared to be smaller than in modern horses, and reminiscent of the third molars paracones and metacones observed in Sussemiones specimens (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The samples were radiocarbon dated to 3456–4460 calibrated years before the present.
source: Combined, these samples were radiocarbon dated to 3456–4460 calibrated years before the present (cal BP), including a mid-second millennium BCE date for the most recent sample, HH13H (3270 ± 30 uncal. BP, i.e., 3456–3616 cal BP) (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by radiocarbon dating results.

claim: The most recent sample, HH13H, was dated to 3270 ± 30 uncal. BP (3456–3616 cal BP).
source: Combined, these samples were radiocarbon dated to 3456–4460 calibrated years before the present (cal BP), including a mid-second millennium BCE date for the most recent sample, HH13H (3270 ± 30 uncal. BP, i.e., 3456–3616 cal BP) (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by radiocarbon dating results.

claim: DNA was extracted from a total of 26 specimens and the whole nuclear genome was sequenced at ~0.002–13.4 times coverage.
source: We extracted ancient DNA from a total of 26 specimens and sequenced the whole nuclear genome at ~0.002–13.4 times coverage, including four samples from Honghe that provided 13.4×, 3.9×, 1.1×, and 1.0× nuclear genome (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is directly supported by the sequencing data.

claim: Comparison of the X chromosome and autosomal coverage revealed the presence of 15 male and 11 female individuals.
source: Comparison of the X chromosome and autosomal coverage revealed the presence of 15 male and 11 female individuals (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of sex chromosomes.

claim: All the Chinese specimens analyzed in this study clustered together along the first two PCA components, in a group that was distinct from all other equine species.
source: All the Chinese specimens analyzed in this study were found to cluster together along the first two PCA components, in a group that was distinct from all other equine species (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) but closer to non-caballine equine species than to the horse (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Chinese specimens clustered closer to non-caballine equine species than to the horse.
source: All the Chinese specimens analyzed in this study were found to cluster together along the first two PCA components, in a group that was distinct from all other equine species (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) but closer to non-caballine equine species than to the horse (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The clustering suggested that all specimens were members of a unique taxonomic group, most related to non-caballine equids.
source: This suggested that they were all members of a unique taxonomic group, most related to non-caballine equids.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA clustering results.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses showed two major mitochondrial clades, of which only one (clade B) was previously characterized.
source: Phylogenetic analyses showed two major clades, of which only one (clade B) was previously characterized. The other clade (A) consisted of two and three individuals from Muzhuzhuliang and Honghe, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Chinese ancient specimens branched off before the radiation leading to modern asses and zebras.
source: This showed that the Chinese ancient specimens branched off before the radiation leading to modern asses and zebras (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The material analyzed represents small specimens of the extinct Equus (Sussemionus) ovodovi.
source: Combined with the analysis of the occlusal surface of the molars, in particular the absence of the caballine notch, the shape of metacones and protocones, and the reduced tooth size (Figure 1B), our analyses consistently supported the material analyzed as small specimens of the extinct Equus (Sussemionus) ovodovi.
evidence: This is supported by morphological and genetic analysis.

claim: The Equus (Sussemionus) ovodovi lineage survived in China during the Holocene until 3477–3637 cal BP.
source: We, thus, concluded that this lineage survived in China during the Holocene, and until 3477–3637 cal BP, which is ~9000 years after the latest known specimen to date (Druzhkova et al., 2017; Orlando et al., 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by radiocarbon dating and genetic analysis.

claim: This survival date is ~9000 years after the latest known specimen to date.
source: We, thus, concluded that this lineage survived in China during the Holocene, and until 3477–3637 cal BP, which is ~9000 years after the latest known specimen to date (Druzhkova et al., 2017; Orlando et al., 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously published dates.

claim: D-statistics detected that E. ovodovi shared an excess of derived polymorphisms with asses relative to zebras.
source: To achieve this, we first applied D-statistics (Soraggi et al., 2018) to the genome sequence underlying 26 individual genomes and detected that E. ovodovi shared an excess of derived polymorphisms with asses than relative to zebras (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by D-statistics analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: At least one admixture event could have taken place between Sussemiones and the ancestor of asses after their divergence from zebras.
source: This suggested that at least one admixture event could have taken place between Sussemiones and the ancestor of asses after their divergence from zebras.
evidence: This is an inference based on D-statistics results.

claim: G-PhoCS analyses confirmed that the zebras and asses lineages diverged ~2.0 Mya.
source: G-PhoCS analyses confirmed previous work indicating that the zebras and asses linages diverged ~2.0 Mya and that the deepest divergence within zebras and asses took place prior to ~1.5 Mya (Jónsson et al., 2014; Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by G-PhoCS analysis shown in Figure 3 and confirmed by citation to Jónsson et al., 2014.

claim: The deepest divergence within zebras and asses took place prior to ~1.5 Mya.
source: G-PhoCS analyses confirmed previous work indicating that the zebras and asses linages diverged ~2.0 Mya and that the deepest divergence within zebras and asses took place prior to ~1.5 Mya (Jónsson et al., 2014; Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by G-PhoCS analysis shown in Figure 3 and confirmed by citation to Jónsson et al., 2014.

claim: G-PhoCS revealed that the Sussemiones lineage diverged from the ancestors of extant non-caballine equids ~2.3–2.7 Mya, in line with the fossil record.
source: It revealed that the Sussemiones lineage diverged from the ancestors of extant non-caballine equids ~2.3–2.7 Mya, in line with the fossil record (Eisenmann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by G-PhoCS analysis and confirmed by citation to Eisenmann, 2010.

claim: G-PhoCS provided support for gene flow between Sussemiones and the ancestor of asses and zebras.
source: Allowing for migrations provided support for gene flow between Sussemiones and the ancestor of asses and zebras (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by G-PhoCS analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: G-PhoCS supported the presence of significant unidirectional gene flow prior to ~2.3–2.7 Mya from the horse branch into the ancestral branch to all non-caballine equids.
source: G-PhoCS also supported the presence of significant unidirectional gene flow prior to ~2.3–2.7 Mya, from the horse branch into the ancestral branch to all non-caballine equids, including Sussemiones (probability of gene flow 2.2–8.8%, Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is supported by G-PhoCS analysis.

claim: The probability of gene flow from the horse branch into the ancestral branch to all non-caballine equids was 2.2–8.8%.
source: G-PhoCS also supported the presence of significant unidirectional gene flow prior to ~2.3–2.7 Mya, from the horse branch into the ancestral branch to all non-caballine equids, including Sussemiones (probability of gene flow 2.2–8.8%, Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is supported by G-PhoCS analysis.

claim: Previous HMMCoal analyses indicated significant gene flow between the deepest branches of the Equus phylogenetic tree until 3.4 Mya.
source: This is consistent with previous HMMCoal analyses applied to whole-genome sequences of all extant equine species, which indicated significant gene flow between the deepest branches of the Equus phylogenetic tree until 3.4 Mya, mostly from a caballine lineage into the ancestor of all non-caballine equids (Jónsson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jónsson et al., 2014.

claim: The PSMC demographic trajectory of Sussemiones diverged from that of other non-caballine equids after ~2.0 Mya.
source: First, the PSMC demographic trajectory of Sussemiones was found to diverge from that of other non-caballine equids (specifically, E. hemionus) after ~2.0 Mya, confirming the divergence date estimate retrieved by G-PhoCS (Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is supported by PSMC analysis.

claim: The Sussemiones demographic trajectory constantly increased during the last million years but remained relatively low for a long period of time until it reached a peak between 74 and 84 kya.
source: Second, the Sussemiones demographic trajectory was found to have constantly increased during the last million year but to have remained relatively low for a long period of time, until it reached a peak between 74 and 84 kya.
evidence: This is supported by PSMC analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Sussemiones demographic trajectory was followed by an ~45-fold collapse until 13 kya after reaching its peak.
source: It was, then, followed by an ~45-fold collapse until 13 kya (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by PSMC analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The lineage maintained extremely reduced population sizes through the Last Glacial Maximum (19–26 kya) and the Holocene until it ultimately became extinct.
source: The lineage maintained extremely reduced population sizes through the Last Glacial Maximal (LGM, 19–26 kya) (Clark et al., 2009) and the Holocene, until it ultimately became extinct.
evidence: This is supported by PSMC analysis and radiocarbon dating.

claim: The sample sequenced to sufficient coverage (HH06D) showed minimal heterozygosity and moderate inbreeding levels.
source: Importantly, the sample sequenced to sufficient coverage (HH06D) showed minimal heterozygosity and moderate inbreeding levels identified by the fraction of the segments within runs of homozygosity (ROH) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by heterozygosity and ROH analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The limited population sizes and resulting genetic diversity, rather than particularly enhanced inbreeding, may have limited the chances of survival of the species and led to extinction.
source: The limited population sizes and resulting genetic diversity, rather than particularly enhanced inbreeding, may, thus, have limited the chances of survival of the species and have ultimately led to extinction.
evidence: This is an inference based on heterozygosity and ROH analysis.

claim: This study characterized the first nuclear genomes of the now-extinct equine lineage, E. (Sussemionus) ovodovi.
source: In this study, we have characterized the first nuclear genomes of the now-extinct equine lineage, E. (Sussemionus) ovodovi, the last surviving member of the subgenus Sussemionus.
evidence: This is directly supported by the genomic sequencing data presented in the study.

claim: E. (Sussemionus) ovodovi is the last surviving member of the subgenus Sussemionus.
source: In this study, we have characterized the first nuclear genomes of the now-extinct equine lineage, E. (Sussemionus) ovodovi, the last surviving member of the subgenus Sussemionus.
evidence: This is based on the fossil record and the dating of specimens.

claim: Sussemionus represents the last currently known Equus subgenus to become extinct.
source: Our work, thus, shows that Sussemionus represents the last currently known Equus subgenus to become extinct.
evidence: This is based on the radiocarbon dating showing survival until ~3500 years ago.

claim: Sussemiones members were still alive at the time horses and donkeys were first domesticated, ~5500 years ago.
source: Our work also adds to the list of recently identified members of the horse family that were still alive at the time horses and donkeys were first domesticated, ~5500 years ago (Fages et al., 2019; Gaunitz et al., 2018; Rossel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on the radiocarbon dating and citations to previous work.

claim: Divergent members identified in Siberia (Equus lenensis) and Iberia (IBE) both belonged to the horse species.
source: In contrast to those divergent members that were identified in Siberia (Equus lenensis) and Iberia (IBE), which both belonged to the horse species (Fages et al., 2019; Schubert et al., 2014a), Sussemiones members were most closely related to non-caballine equids.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fages et al., 2019; Schubert et al., 2014a.

claim: This study solved the question of the exact phylogenetic placement of Sussemiones by reporting the first whole-genome phylogeny.
source: Our study solved this question by reporting the first whole-genome phylogeny of Sussemiones, which confirmed with maximal bootstrap support this species as a basal lineage of non-caballine equids.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis with maximal bootstrap support.

claim: The whole-genome phylogeny confirmed with maximal bootstrap support that Sussemiones is a basal lineage of non-caballine equids.
source: Our study solved this question by reporting the first whole-genome phylogeny of Sussemiones, which confirmed with maximal bootstrap support this species as a basal lineage of non-caballine equids.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Previous research indicated an ecological range for Sussemiones overlapping with grasslands located east of the Altay Mountains and west of the Yenisei River during the Late Pleistocene.
source: Previous zooarchaeological and environmental research indicated an ecological range for Sussemiones overlapping with the grasslands located east of the Altay Mountains and west of the Yenisei River during the Late Pleistocene (Khenzykhenova et al., 2016; Malikov, 2016; Plasteeva et al., 2015; Shchetnikov et al., 2015; Slon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent research reported Sussemiones occurrence in northeastern China (~12,600–40,200 YBP) where similar climatic and ecological conditions were found.
source: Recent research also reported species occurrence in northeastern China (~12,600–40,200 YBP), where similar climatic and ecological conditions were found at the time (Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2019.

claim: It could be speculated that Sussemiones were adapted to an environment with moderately dry climatic conditions and steppe landscapes.
source: It could, thus, be speculated that Sussemiones were adapted to an environment with moderately dry climatic conditions and steppe landscapes (Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous research.

claim: This study identified Sussemiones specimens in three late Holocene sites from China characterized by mild and humid environmental conditions.
source: However, our study identified Sussemiones specimens in three late Holocene sites from China characterized by mild and humid environmental conditions.
evidence: This is based on the archaeological and environmental context of the sites.

claim: Two distinct mitochondrial haplogroups from 22 individuals have been defined from the six known sites, suggesting possible population structure across various geographic areas.
source: Additionally, two distinct mitochondrial haplogroups from 22 individuals have been defined from the six known sites, suggesting possible population structure across various geographic areas and adaptation to local environments.
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The species could adapt to a wider variety of habitats than previously hypothesized.
source: It also suggests that the species could adapt to a wider variety of habitats than previously hypothesized and rejects the contention that the species became extinct as it could not survive in warmer climatic conditions (Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the environmental context of the sites and the survival dates.

claim: This study rejects the contention that the species became extinct as it could not survive in warmer climatic conditions.
source: It also suggests that the species could adapt to a wider variety of habitats than previously hypothesized and rejects the contention that the species became extinct as it could not survive in warmer climatic conditions (Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the environmental context of the sites and the survival dates.

claim: The geographic range of E. ovodovi was larger than previously expected and included at least Northern China and Southern Siberia.
source: This implies that the geographic range of E. ovodovi was larger than previously expected and included at least Northern China and Southern Siberia.
evidence: This is based on the geographic distribution of the specimens analyzed.

claim: Given the lack of mitochondrial phylogeographic structure, it could be speculated that Northern China and Southern Siberia were in contact at least maternally.
source: Although in the absence of identified fossils from Mongolia, given that there is a lack of mitochondrial phylogeographic structure, we could speculate that the two regions were in contact at least maternally.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the lack of phylogeographic structure.

claim: After the peak of population size culminating ~74 kya, Sussemiones went through a slow and continuous decline until 13 kya.
source: The demographic profile of Sussemiones shows that after the peak of population size culminating ~74 kya, Sussemiones went through a slow and continuous decline until 13 kya (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by PSMC analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: This time period encompasses several major climate changes (especially the LGM, ~19–26 kya) and the great human expansion to Eurasia (~35–45 kya).
source: This time period encompasses several major climate changes (especially the LGM, ~19–26 kya) (Clark et al., 2009) and the great human expansion to Eurasia (~35–45 kya) (Henn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2009 and Henn et al., 2012.

claim: The reduced genetic diversity available in the lineage may have compromised the long-term survival of the lineage, in a process partly reminiscent of what was previously described for the woolly mammoth.
source: As the inbreeding levels were not particularly high compared to some members of endangered equine species (Figure 5), the reduced genetic diversity available in the lineage may have compromised the long-term survival of the lineage, in a process partly reminiscent of what was previously described for the woolly mammoth (Palkopoulou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on heterozygosity and ROH analysis, with a citation to Palkopoulou et al., 2015.

claim: Considering the rapid expansion of domestic horses across Eurasia from about 2000 BC, the Sussemiones lineage was ultimately replaced under growing anthropogenic stress.
source: And considering the rapid expansion of domestic horses across Eurasia from about 2000 BC (Librado et al., 2021), this lineage was ultimately replaced under growing anthropogenic stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of extinction and the expansion of domestic horses, with a citation to Librado et al., 2021.

claim: This study clarifies the phylogenetic placement, speciation timing, and evolutionary history of the now-extinct Sussemionus equine subgenus.
source: In conclusion, our study clarifies the phylogenetic placement, speciation timing, and evolutionary history of the now-extinct Sussemionus equine subgenus.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Sussemionus did not remain in reproductive isolation from other equine lineages but contributed to the genetic makeup of the ancestors of present-day asses.
source: This group did not remain in reproductive isolation from other equine lineages, but contributed to the genetic makeup of the ancestors of present-day asses, while receiving genetic material from the ancestors of African zebras.
evidence: This is supported by D-statistics and G-PhoCS analyses showing evidence of admixture.

claim: Sussemionus received genetic material from the ancestors of African zebras.
source: This group did not remain in reproductive isolation from other equine lineages, but contributed to the genetic makeup of the ancestors of present-day asses, while receiving genetic material from the ancestors of African zebras.
evidence: This is supported by G-PhoCS analyses showing evidence of admixture.

claim: The admixture supports geographic distributions at least partly overlapping at the time, thus not identical to those observed today.
source: This supports geographic distributions at least partly overlapping at the time, thus, not identical to those observed today.
evidence: This is an inference based on the admixture evidence.

claim: The species demographic trajectory experienced a steady decline from ~74 kya during a period witnessing both important climatic changes and the Great human expansion across Asia.
source: The species demographic trajectory experienced a steady decline from ~74 kya and during a period witnessing both important climatic changes and the Great human expansion across Asia (Henn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by PSMC analysis and citation to Henn et al., 2012.

claim: Sussemiones survived with minimal genetic diversity the Pleistocene-Holocene transition and for at least eight millennia before it became extinct.
source: It survived with minimal genetic diversity the Pleistocene-Holocene transition, and for at least eight millennia before it became extinct, which provides insights into the survival potential of large animals since the Holocene.
evidence: This is supported by heterozygosity analysis and radiocarbon dating.

claim: The persistence of Sussemiones throughout the third and second millennia BCE means archaeologists must be exceedingly careful while assigning Asian zooarchaeological material to equine taxa until this period.
source: Given the persistence of Sussemiones throughout the third and second millennia BCE, archaeologists must be exceedingly careful while assigning Asian zooarchaeological material to equine taxa until this period.
evidence: This is an inference based on the survival dates and the implications for archaeological interpretation.

claim: MNI was estimated to 31 individuals at Honghe, 4 at Muzhuzhuliang, and 4 at Shatangbeiyuan.
source: MNI was estimated to 31 individuals at Honghe, 4 at Muzhuzhuliang, and 4 at Shatangbeiyuan.
evidence: This is based on archaeological analysis of the specimens.

claim: DNA preservation conditions were compatible with the recovery of ancient DNA sequences from only 20 of the 31 Honghe samples, 3 of the 4 Muzhuzhuliang samples, and 3 of the 4 Shatangbeiyuan samples.
source: DNA preservation conditions were compatible with the recovery of ancient DNA sequences from only 20 of the 31 Honghe samples, 3 of the 4 Muzhuzhuliang samples, and 3 of the 4 Shatangbeiyuan samples (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is based on DNA extraction and sequencing results.
